title: How to run a customer education team of one
summary: What a one-person customer education team should own, hand to experts, and give to AI, using Teamworks' growth from 2 to 20+ products as the example.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


- A one-person education team can't record, narrate, and edit every video for a product line that keeps growing. At Teamworks, each education person went from covering two products in 2021 to about seven in 2026.
- Hand recording to the people who know the product. A raw walkthrough narrated the way an expert explains it on a customer call carries detail you'd lose in a written handoff.
- Let AI take the production work and put the hours you get back into review. Teamworks now makes about three times as many videos in under a third of the production hours.
- Fix the update cost before you add videos. A change that has to be made in four tools gets made four times, so get every video down to one source you edit once.
- Write your standards down where software can apply them, and report feature adoption instead of video counts. Teamworks' academy users adopt key features about three times more than users who skip it.


In 2021, Zach Romash was the entire customer education function at Teamworks, a software company that runs operations for elite sports teams. The company sold two products. By the middle of 2026 the suite, which kept growing through acquisition, had passed 20 products, and his team had grown to three people. Divide one number by the other and each person now covers about seven products, each shipping changes on its own schedule.


Hiring alone doesn't close that gap, and Teamworks' team grew far more slowly than its product list. What changed was the job itself. Zach stopped recording and narrating every video, moved production into one tool, wrote his standards down where software could apply them, and started reporting what customers did after watching. The[Teamworks customer story](https://www.clueso.io/customers/teamworks) has the before-and-after numbers, and they're worth reading closely, because they show where a small team's hours go once AI takes over production.


If you run customer education alone, I think your job is to set the standards and review what ships, while product experts record and AI does the production work in between. The rest of this post makes that case with Teamworks' numbers and turns each part into something you can set up this month.


## Products grow faster than education teams, so the job has to change


Each new product adds screens to teach, and releases keep changing the old ones. An education team's workload is roughly the number of products multiplied by how often each one changes, and neither number waits for a headcount approval. At Teamworks the first number went up about tenfold in five years while the team tripled.


The pressure shows up in how teams shop for tools. On the first sales calls we held between January and August 2026, 30% of teams named keeping their existing videos up to date as a reason for looking, about three times its share in 2024.


Before you change anything, measure your own version of the ratio. List every product or major module you support, and next to each one, write how many releases last quarter changed something a customer sees. Then estimate how many of your existing videos each of those releases touched. That total is the maintenance load your one person is carrying before a single new video gets made, and it's the number to bring to your manager.


If you're planning how the team should grow from here, our Cluebook chapter on[building your customer education team](https://www.clueso.io/cluebooks/building-a-customer-education-program--building-your-customer-education-team) maps the roles by company stage.


## Product experts should record, and you should stop narrating


At two products, Zach could be the voice of everything. At 20, he couldn't be an expert in all of them, which meant every video depended on him learning a workflow someone else knew better.


Teamworks moved recording to the product success team. Each product expert now has their own account and records a raw walkthrough, narrated the way they'd talk a customer through the task on a call. They don't write a script, stage the screen, or edit anything. The recording goes to the education team, which turns it into the finished video.


The bigger effect is on quality. An expert narrating live mentions the setting customers always miss and the error message that means something else, because they've answered those questions all quarter. A written brief loses most of that.


Our own product data points the same way. In a study of videos built with Clueso's AI chat,[requests that came with an uploaded recording were exported 17.3% of the time](https://www.clueso.io/blog/ai-in-customer-education) , against 4.3% for requests with a prompt alone. Videos that start from someone doing the real task were about four times as likely to be finished.


Getting good raw recordings takes a short, specific ask. Give the expert a demo account with stable sample data, so the next re-record shows the same customer and the same numbers. Keep each recording to one task a customer actually asks about. Tell them to talk to a customer, not to a camera, and not to restart when they fumble a sentence, because the narration gets cleaned up afterwards.


On those terms, a recording takes the expert about as long as the task itself. Teamworks' product marketers went a step further and now make their own GIFs and short clips for newsletters, work that used to land on the education team.


## AI should take the production hours, and review should get them back


The published Teamworks numbers make a useful sum. Before the change, the team made three to five videos a month at 4–5 hours each, which is roughly 12–25 hours of production a month. Afterwards it made 10–15 videos a month at 20–30 minutes each, roughly 3–8 hours. At the midpoints of those ranges, that's about three times the output in under a third of the production time.


The interesting part is where the rest of those hours went. Teamworks rebuilt one product's set of roughly eight courses in about six weeks, against an estimated 3–4 months under the old pipeline, and 70–80% of its products now have an onboarding course behind them. Those are the projects a team of one never had time for, and the published numbers suggest that's where much of the saved time went.


They should also go into review. A video built in minutes still needs someone who knows the product to watch it end to end before it ships, and that's now the slowest step for most teams. Review against a short list: the steps are in the order a customer would do them, product names match the current UI, the sample data shows nothing real, and the zooms land on the click the narration describes. If a check fails, fix that part rather than regenerating the whole video.


Teamworks runs this workflow in Clueso. The expert[records the workflow](https://www.clueso.io/features/screen-recorder) and narrates it roughly, and Clueso turns the narration into a clean script, an[AI voiceover](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) , zooms and captions, and a[step-by-step guide](https://www.clueso.io/documentation) from the same recording. Most of Teamworks' videos now start in Claude through the[Clueso MCP](https://www.clueso.io/mcp) , which is on every plan. The team names the[Clueprint](https://www.clueso.io/clueprints) that holds the product's template, uploads the raw recording, and lists the edits and callouts it wants, then opens Clueso only for final touches.


Community Clueprints are on every plan, and custom Clueprints built around your own brand are on Enterprise. A video can also start from a document, a slide deck, or a prompt when there's no recording to work from.


## Fix the update cost before you make another video


Teamworks' old pipeline ran through four tools: a screen recorder, a separate AI voice tool, slides for the title cards, and Premiere for the final edit. Then the company rebranded, and colors and product names changed across a suite that was still growing. Every correction had to be made in all four places, for every video that already existed. Keeping up was close to impossible.


The cost showed up somewhere less visible too. Customer success would ask for videos about specific use cases, and the education team had to turn many of them down, because five hours of editing was hard to justify for a video the next release might break. So the expensive update path cost Teamworks the use-case videos customer success kept asking for. Once every change became one edit and a regenerate, video started shipping with each product update instead of being rationed.


Count the update surface for one of your own videos. Note every tool the video passes through, every language it exists in, every page where it's embedded, and the written guide that goes with it. Each of those is a place a single product change has to be fixed.


Then work the number down. Keep the script separate from the capture, so a renamed button is a text edit, and build longer videos from short clips, so one changed step means one replaced clip. Publishing by embed means a fix appears everywhere at once.


Translations work the same way when you generate them from the script, because they[follow the English version](https://www.clueso.io/features/auto-translate) instead of being redone by hand. When Teamworks rolled out a new unified mobile app, it shipped Dutch and Spanish versions of the onboarding tutorials in time for teams to teach their players.


Our guide to[updating a training video without re-recording it](https://www.clueso.io/blog/update-training-video-without-re-recording) covers each kind of change step by step, and the post on[why maintaining product videos now costs more than making them](https://www.clueso.io/blog/product-video-maintenance-cost) works through the yearly sum. If a rebrand is coming, start with[finding every video and doc that still shows the old branding](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-to-find-and-replace-old-brand-assets-after-a-rebrand) .


## Standards only work when they're written where software can apply them


Three people producing video across 20 products will drift. Product names creep back to their pre-acquisition versions, and each person ends up zooming on clicks a little differently. Zach treated this as a management problem first, and the fix was to write the standard down where other people, and software, could apply it.


Teamworks wrote its standards down in two places. The first is a template per product, so the brand and format are decided once per product instead of once per video. The second is a set of instructions their AI assistant follows on every build, covering things like where zooms should land relative to the narration and which product terms to use.


Early on, someone had to repair zooms by hand after every video. The written rules took that work over, and they improve every time the team adds a correction to them.


You can write the first version in an afternoon. Put your product names and the terms customers should hear on one page, along with your intro and outro, caption style, where zooms and callouts go, and the maximum length for each kind of video. Then move that page into the places that apply it automatically, which means your[video templates](https://www.clueso.io/clueprints) and the instructions you give your AI assistant. From then on, review checks whether a video is right rather than whether it matches last month's.


## Report feature adoption, because video counts make the case against you


If you report how many videos you shipped, you're making a case against your own headcount, because AI now makes a video in about 20 minutes. Our post on[what AI is really changing in customer education](https://www.clueso.io/blog/ai-in-customer-education) argues that the request should be for expert hours and review time. The number that supports that request is what customers do after they watch.


Teamworks tracks academy completion against what people do in the product afterwards. Users who go through the academy adopt key features about three times more than users who don't. The academy is now 90% video, which suits an audience of athletes who mostly watch on a phone and don't engage much with help articles. A threefold difference on the features that make a product sticky is a number a revenue leader can act on.


Start small. For one product, pick the handful of features that predict whether a customer stays, then compare customers who completed the related course with those who didn't over their first 30 days. Report that monthly next to your maintenance load from the first section. Our Cluebook chapter on[metrics to track](https://www.clueso.io/cluebooks/building-a-customer-education-program--metrics-to-track) covers the rest of the dashboard, and[how to keep up with a fast-moving product with a small CE team](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-to-keep-up-with-a-fast-moving-product-with-a-small-ce-team) covers deciding which releases need a video at all.


## Frequently asked questions


### What kinds of AI video platforms help customer education teams create tutorials?


Look for a platform that starts from a product expert's screen recording, a document, or a slide deck, and turns it into a finished video with an AI voiceover, zooms, captions, and a written step-by-step guide. Clueso does all of that from one recording, with brand templates called Clueprints so several creators produce consistent videos. Teams working in Claude or ChatGPT can also build videos through the Clueso MCP, which is on every plan.


### Which video tools work best for customer education teams updating tutorials after frequent product changes?


Pick a tool where the script stays editable after the video is made, so a renamed button is a text edit and a regenerated voiceover rather than a re-recording. Videos built from short clips and published by embed make each fix one change that appears everywhere. In Clueso you edit the script or replace the clip that changed, and on the Enterprise plan, Clueso Agents can re-record changed workflows in a demo account after a release, with a person reviewing each update.


### How can customer education teams turn expert walkthroughs or recorded calls into reusable videos?


Ask the product expert to record the task once in a demo account, narrating it the way they'd explain it to a customer. The AI then cleans the narration into a script and adds the voiceover, zooms, and captions. You can upload a recorded call instead, but a clean screen recording of the task produces a clearer video. Teamworks moved its recording to product experts this way, and its education team now polishes and reviews rather than records.


### How much do video tools cost for a small customer education team?


Clueso's Free plan exports 10 minutes of video a month with a watermark and no credit card. Solo is $40 a month billed yearly for one person, and Business is $120 a month billed yearly for two users, with more seats available. Enterprise is priced on request and adds custom Clueprints, SSO, SCORM export, and Clueso Agents. Current details are on the[pricing page](https://www.clueso.io/pricing) .


Pick the product that changed most last quarter and ask its product expert for one 10-minute raw recording of the task customers ask about most. Time how long it takes you to turn that recording into a finished, reviewed video and its written guide. If it's under an hour, you can hand recording over this month. If it's longer, start with the update surface, because every video you make before fixing it adds to the load you're already behind on.
